strengths: Clear motivation and systematic decomposition of visual token redundancy into intra-modal diversity (within visual tokens) and inter-modal relevance (between vision and language).
Extensive experimental evaluation across four diverse LVLM backbones (LLaVA-NeXT-7B/13B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and InternVL2-8B) on 12 benchmarks covering both image and video modalities.

Strong empirical performance: under severe compression (10% token retention), ToDRE preserves 95% of the unpruned model accuracy while achieving real latency and memory reductions, consistently outperforming recent baselines such as DivPrune and FasterVLM.
The observation of 'information migration' across LLM decoder layers is well-substantiated empirically and offers a simple, training-free mechanism to completely drop visual tokens in deeper layers.
weaknesses: The novelty over existing diversity-based methods (particularly DivPrune [2]) is somewhat incremental: Stage 1 adapts a max-sum diversification heuristic with a CLS pivot, which is conceptually very close to existing diversity-driven pruning strategies.

The practical efficiency gain brought by Stage 2 is relatively modest on standard VQA benchmarks. As demonstrated in Table 5, adding Stage 2 on top of Stage 1 reduces total runtime by only ~5% (from 31:18 to 29:43 at 10% retention) because visual tokens have already been heavily pruned in Stage 1 and benchmark answers are mostly short phrases.

The theoretical justification presented in Section 2 of the Supplementary Material is unconvincing: asserting Lemma 1 (sub-space independence) by postulating that orthogonal subspace decomposition implies statistical independence between arbitrary pairwise visual similarity kernels and text-visual redundancy functions lacks rigorous justification and feels artificially tacked on.

The layer selection criterion in Stage 2 appears to function almost as a static layer drop (fixed at fractional depth 7L/8). The paper lacks analysis on how frequently the threshold condition fails across different benchmarks or samples.

strengths: Clear motivation and systematic decomposition of visual token redundancy into intra-modal diversity (within visual tokens) and cross-modal relevance (between visual and textual tokens).

Extensive and thorough experimental validation across four distinct LVLM architectures (LLaVA-NeXT-7B/13B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, InternVL2-8B) across twelve diverse multimodal benchmarks spanning both image and video comprehension.

Strong empirical performance under aggressive compression rates: retains 95.0% performance on LLaVA-NeXT-7B with only 10% visual tokens preserved, consistently outperforming recent training-free baselines like FastV, FasterVLM, and DivPrune.
The proposed method is training-free, architecture-agnostic, and plug-and-play, maintaining compatibility with standard inference workflows.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Stage 1 relies on greedy max-sum diversification which is conceptually very close to prior diversity-based token selection methods such as DivPrune, with only minor heuristic variations (e.g., [CLS]-based pivot initialization). Stage 2 (late-layer token dropping based on fading cross-modal attention) is also closely related to visual token withdrawal concepts explored in works like VTW.

The theoretical justification in Supplementary Section 2 appears somewhat superficial and artificial: it assumes an orthogonal subspace condition ($W_V^\top W_T = 0$) and asserts independence between intra- and cross-modal metrics, which does not strictly hold in standard LVLM projector and embedding spaces where modalities are projected into a shared semantic space to enable cross-attention.

Marginal practical contribution of Stage 2 in the evaluated benchmarks: As shown in Table 5, adding Stage 2 on top of Stage 1 reduces wall-clock time only slightly (e.g., 31:18 to 29:43 at 10% ratio) because 90% of tokens are already removed in Stage 1 and standard benchmarks have short answer lengths.

Lack of detailed discussion on the wall-clock computational overhead of the iterative greedy selection algorithm (Algorithm 1) during the pre-LLM phase, especially as token counts scale with higher-resolution dynamic tiling or many-frame video inputs.

strengths: Clear motivation: Decoupling visual token reduction into intra-modal redundancy (handled via diversity in the embedding space) and cross-modal redundancy (handled via attention-based layer-wise dropping) provides a clean, principled conceptual framing.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The proposed method is evaluated across four widely used LVLMs (LLaVA-NeXT-7B, LLaVA-NeXT-13B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2-8B) across twelve diverse benchmarks spanning both image and video understanding.

Training-free and hardware-friendly: The method operates without retraining or fine-tuning, is compatible with FlashAttention, and demonstrates solid practical wall-clock time reduction and memory savings on real hardware (RTX 3090).

Detailed ablation studies: The paper provides informative ablations analyzing the contribution of each stage, the pivot selection strategy, the threshold parameter $\tau$, and the layer depth selection.
weaknesses: Incremental novelty: Both key components share substantial similarities with prior literature. Diversity-driven token selection is very closely related to DivPrune (which also uses dissimilarity-based greedy selection), and late-layer token pruning based on diminishing attention/information migration builds directly upon observations from FastV and VTW.

Superficial theoretical analysis: The theoretical justification in Section 2 of the supplementary material relies on an unrealistic assumption of linear orthogonal subspace decomposition ($W_V^\top W_T = 0$) and asserts statistical independence (Lemma 1) without formal proof for non-linear kernels. The theoretical derivation feels somewhat contrived rather than offering rigorous foundational insight.

Marginal efficiency contribution from Stage 2: As shown in the ablation study (Table 5), adding Stage 2 on top of Stage 1 reduces runtime only from 31:18 to 29:43 at the 10% retention ratio. Because pruning occurs very late in the network ($7L/8$) and the evaluated QA benchmarks primarily require short answers, the actual practical acceleration provided by Stage 2 is minimal.

Lack of quantitative evaluation on long-form generation: The authors hypothesize that Stage 2 provides major benefits in long-generation settings where decoding latency dominates. However, the quantitative evaluation is restricted to benchmarks with short or multiple-choice answers, missing quantitative evaluations on long-form captioning or multi-turn dialogue.

Latency overhead of greedy selection: Algorithm 1 involves an iterative selection loop over $k$ steps across $n$ tokens. For high-resolution dynamic tiling or multi-frame video inputs where $n$ is large, the CPU/GPU runtime overhead of computing and updating cumulative cosine similarities is not explicitly decoupled or quantified.

strengths: The paper provides a clear and intuitive motivation by disentangling token redundancy into intra-modal redundancy (addressed via diversity) and cross-modal redundancy (addressed via task-relevance and information migration).

Extensive experimental evaluation across 12 benchmarks covering both image and video understanding tasks, demonstrating solid performance retention (95.1% on average under 90% token pruning on LLaVA-NeXT-7B).
The proposed method is training-free and plug-and-play, maintaining compatibility with standard inference frameworks and attention implementations.
Comprehensive ablation studies analyzing the impact of both pruning stages, the layer candidate selection, and threshold hyperparameter sensitivity.
weaknesses: Limited architectural diversity: The experimental validation is restricted exclusively to LLaVA-NeXT (7B and 13B). Evaluating modern architectures with distinct vision projectors and native dynamic resolution mechanisms (such as Qwen2-VL or InternVL2) is needed to verify generalizability.

Marginal efficiency gains from Stage 2: As indicated in Table 3 and Table 4, the throughput and latency improvements contributed by Stage 2 over existing baselines (e.g., FasterVLM) and over Stage 1 alone are quite incremental (e.g., throughput increases from 2.7 to 2.8 samples/s; inference time decreases from 30:38 to 29:31).

Overhead of the greedy k-center selection: The greedy k-center expansion incurs O(k·n·d) operations on CPU/GPU. A detailed wall-clock breakdown quantifying the exact runtime of the Stage 1 selection algorithm itself is missing.

The theoretical proof in Appendix B relies on strong, idealized assumptions (such as strict subspace orthogonality W_V^T W_T = 0 and independence between features), which do not necessarily reflect the coupled representation dynamics of practical transformer layers.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across a broad benchmark suite: The method is validated on twelve image and video benchmarks (e.g., MME, ScienceQA, POPE, VideoMME, EgoSchema) across two parameter scales (LLaVA-NeXT 7B and 13B), demonstrating consistent retention of accuracy under aggressive compression ratios (down to 10% tokens).

Sound conceptual motivation: Decomposing redundancy into intra-modal visual diversity (via greedy k-center sampling) and cross-modal task relevance addresses recognized pitfalls of pure attention-score ranking, such as positional bias and token clustering.
Completely training-free and plug-and-play: The method requires neither fine-tuning nor offline calibration datasets, allowing direct integration into existing pre-trained LVLM inference pipelines.
Clear writing and well-structured ablations: The paper provides informative ablations regarding the threshold τ, layer selection heuristics, and the individual contributions of Stage 1 and Stage 2.
weaknesses: Evaluation restricted to a single model family: Experiments are conducted exclusively on LLaVA-NeXT (Vicuna LLM + CLIP ViT). Validating the approach across other contemporary architectures with different projectors and encoders (e.g., Qwen2-VL, InternVL, or SigLIP-based models) is needed to substantiate general applicability.

Marginal efficiency gains over strong baselines: In Table 3, compared to FasterVLM, the throughput increases only from 2.7 to 2.8 samples/s and FLOPs decrease from 6.1T to 6.0T. The primary empirical advantage lies in task accuracy preservation rather than a substantial computational speedup relative to prior token pruning approaches.

Potential degradation on visually grounded, long-form generation: In Stage 2, all visual tokens are completely eliminated once cross-modal attention falls below a threshold. While this functions well on standard multiple-choice and short-answer benchmarks, completely dropping visual KV states may impair long-form generation tasks where the model must continuously refer back to fine visual details.

Theoretical proof in Appendix B relies on strong idealized assumptions: The theoretical justification assumes strict modal subspace orthogonality (W_V^T W_T = 0) by construction, which does not necessarily reflect the non-linear, shared latent representations learned in actual LVLM projector layers.

strengths: Clear motivation and intuitive design: The paper correctly identifies key limitations of pure attention-score-based pruning (such as causal decoding positional bias and over-concentration) and provides an intuitive two-stage compression scheme that balances intra-modal visual diversity with cross-modal task relevance.

Extensive experimental validation: The method is benchmarked across twelve diverse image and video comprehension benchmarks (including MME, ScienceQA, GQA, POPE, VideoMME, EgoSchema, etc.) and across two model scales (7B and 13B), demonstrating consistent accuracy improvements over existing training-free baselines (e.g., FastV, FasterVLM, GlobalCom2) under heavy pruning ratios (10% and 25%).

Detailed empirical analysis and ablation studies: The paper provides clear wall-clock time, FLOPs, and peak memory evaluations, alongside comprehensive ablations on pruning thresholds and layer selection schedules.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: The individual components are adaptations of well-known techniques. Stage 1 employs greedy k-center clustering (essentially classic Farthest Point Sampling / FPS) using [CLS] attention as a seed, which has been widely explored in vision transformers and point cloud processing. Stage 2 (dropping visual tokens in deeper LLM layers based on attention diminishing) is heavily inspired by and closely follows prior work like VTW (Lin et al., 2025).

Dubious theoretical justification in Appendix B: The theoretical derivation of 'orthogonality' between intra- and cross-modal redundancy explicitly assumes $W_V^\top W_T = 0$ as an enforced condition. In standard LVLMs (such as LLaVA-NeXT), visual and textual embeddings are projected into a shared semantic latent space without any explicit subspace orthogonality constraint, rendering the theoretical proof disconnected from actual model architectures.

Runtime overhead and scalability of greedy k-center: The sequential nature of greedy k-center selection (Algorithm 1) involves $k$ sequential iterations of finding the maximum similarity token and updating distances. Although total inference time is reported, the paper does not isolate the algorithmic overhead of this selection process, which can become a bottleneck when scaling to larger batch sizes or higher input resolutions with thousands of patches.

Evaluation limited to a single LVLM family: All experiments are conducted solely on LLaVA-NeXT (7B and 13B), which relies on Vicuna. Validating the approach on more modern architectures with different RoPE mechanisms and dynamic resolution paradigms (e.g., Qwen2-VL or InternVL2) is necessary to substantiate claims of general applicability across LVLMs.
